title: Resource tier floors (ACP-SPEC-001 §8.3.2, RK-1)
description:
Maps each governable resource to its floor tier.

RK-1: a resource ABSENT from this file MUST be treated as T3. That rule cannot be expressed in JSON Schema — a schema constrains what is present, never what is missing — so it is carried instead by the `x-acp-absent` annotation on `floors` below, which `tools/codegen.sh` reads to GENERATE the fail-safe direction into `Tier::for_unclassified()` (crates/acp-core) and its TypeScript equivalent. The Python reference spells the same default at `acp_executor.py`. A conformance case asserts it, because a fail-safe default that only exists in a comment is not a control — and stating it only in this prose is what let the Rust and TypeScript versions return HIGH, a RISK LEVEL, where a TIER was required.

RES-1 (A-7): the architecture guarantees no runtime component evaluates a resource BELOW its signed floor. It cannot know whether the floor was set correctly. A production database labelled T0 defeats the design with zero attack. Floor maintenance is the highest-leverage governance task in the system and is structurally unprovable — this file is where that risk concentrates.

floors.description: resource identifier -> floor tier. Deliberately an open map: resources are deployment-specific. The VALUES are closed.

x-acp-absent.why: absent means unknown, and unknown is the HIGHEST tier, not the lowest (P-4). Returning T0 or T1 here is the whole class of defect this specification exists to prevent, and it is the direction a lookup returning `Option` invites.

tier.description: T0 public/sandbox · T1 internal · T2 production · T3 privileged. Ordered: T0 < T1 < T2 < T3, and §8.4 composes tiers with max, so the ordering is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.
